title: Sparse Attention Is Matrix Approximation, Not Choosing from a Bag of Values

paper.title: Sparse Attention Is Matrix Approximation, Not Choosing from a Bag of Values
paper.abstract: Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve strong performance across many domains, but their efficiency is limited by the quadratic cost of attention with respect to prompt length. Sparse attention reduces this cost by retaining only a small fraction of query-key interactions to approximate the full attention matrix. However, existing methods are trapped in a mathematically wrong view: they simply keep large scalar entries or high-mass regions of the attention matrix. This treats the attention matrix as a bag of values, ignoring that it is used as a structured matrix whose entries jointly determine the attention output through multiplication with value vectors. We argue that this is the core conceptual issue: sparse attention should be formulated as matrix approximation, not as blindly choosing the largest values from a bag of entries. Based on this view, we propose M atrix A pproximation S parse A ttention ( MASA ). MASA replaces raw attention-mass ranking with a closed-form score that measures how much each sparse unit reduces matrix-product approximation error. As a theory-grounded plug-in correction, MASA can be added to existing sparse attention frameworks without changing their sparse kernels or budgets. Extensive experiments across multiple sparse attention methods, benchmarks, and LLM backbones show consistent accuracy gains, supporting both MASA and the matrix-approximation view of sparse attention.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across a wide range of applications, from natural language processing ( Radford et al., 2018 ) to mathematical reasoning ( Ahn et al., 2024 ) , multimodal tasks ( Team et al., 2023 ) , and scientific discovery ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) . However, efficiency remains a central challenge for LLMs ( Bai et al., 2024a ) . As tasks become more complex and prompts become more structured, the input length continues to grow rapidly ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . Since attention computation has quadratic complexity with respect to the prompt length ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) , attention becomes a major bottleneck for efficient long-context inference. Sparse attention is a natural way to reduce this cost while keeping the main modeling benefit of attention. Prior work has observed that attention matrices often contain sparse and structured patterns ( Jiang et al., 2024a ) , suggesting that only a small fraction of query-key interactions is needed to approximate full attention. Based on this observation, many methods select a sparse subset of the attention matrix under a compute budget. Early approaches use fixed or predefined patterns: Sliding Window Attention ( Jiang et al., 2023a ) restricts each query to a local context window, while MInference ( Jiang et al., 2024a ) approximates attention using vertical lines, slash lines, and blocks. Other methods make the selection input-aware: SeerAttention ( Gao et al., 2025 ) learns to predict block-sparse attention patterns, and Quest ( Tang et al., 2024 ) retrieves query-aware key pages. More recent methods further adapt the sparse budget, such as FlexPrefill ( Lai et al., 2025 ) , which decides when to stop selecting additional sparse units, and Tactic ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , which adjusts the budget through clustering and distribution fitting. Despite these different designs, the final selection rule remains ultimately magnitude-driven: sparse attention methods keep large scalar entries or high-mass regions of the attention matrix. This selection principle has a mathematical mismatch. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , a candidate with much larger mass can preserve the matrix product substantially worse under the same sparse budget. Magnitude-based selection treats the attention matrix as a bag of scalar values, whereas Transformers use it as a structured matrix acting on value vectors through matrix multiplication ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) . Therefore, the right question is not which entries of the attention matrix are largest, but which selected entries best preserve the matrix product that produces the attention output. In other words, sparse attention should be formulated as matrix approximation, not as blindly choosing the largest values from a bag of entries. Based on this view, we propose M atrix A pproximation S parse A ttention ( MASA ), a theory-grounded plug-in correction for sparse attention. MASA keeps the sparse units, kernels, and budgets of existing sparse attention methods, but replaces their raw attention-mass ranking with a closed-form score derived from matrix-product approximation error. This changes the selection target from preserving large entries of the attention matrix to preserving the matrix action that determines the attention output. As a result, MASA can be added to diverse sparse attention frameworks without changing their implementation interface. Figure 1: A minimal two-column counterexample. Under the same one-column budget, conventional mass-based ranking selects u 1 u_{1} , whose mass is 66 × 66\times larger but incurs 98 % 98\% relative matrix-product error. MASA selects u 2 u_{2} and reduces the error to 3 % 3\% . Here, 𝑿 {\bm{X}} is an illustrative probe matrix. In this work, our contributions are summarized as follows: • Theory. We identify a long-standing selection mismatch in sparse attention: existing magnitude-based rules approximate the attention matrix entrywise, while the Transformer uses attention through matrix multiplication. We provide a matrix-approximation view that gives the correct selection objective. • Method. We propose MASA, a theory-grounded plug-in scoring method that ranks sparse units by their closed-form reduction in matrix-product approximation error. MASA can be integrated into existing sparse attention baselines while keeping their sparse kernels and budgets unchanged. • Experiments. We evaluate MASA across multiple sparse attention methods, benchmarks, and LLM backbones. Under matched settings with the original baselines, MASA gives consistent accuracy gains, supporting both the proposed method and the matrix-approximation view of sparse attention.

sections.heading: 2 Preliminaries
sections.text: We review sparse attention methods through three representative frameworks used to evaluate MASA, then formalize sparse attention. Broader LLM acceleration methods are discussed in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 2.1 Related Work
sections.text: MInference ( Jiang et al., 2024a ) is a training-free framework that exploits multiple structured patterns through offline head-wise assignment . It searches among A-shaped, vertical-slash, and block-sparse patterns for each attention head. The assigned pattern type and budget remain fixed, while sparse indices are constructed dynamically for each input. MoA ( Fu et al., 2025 ) similarly uses offline configuration, but sets head- and layer-specific sliding-window spans. SeerAttention ( Gao et al., 2025 ) instead learns input-dependent sparse layouts within a block-based representation . GPU-friendly blocks can approximate different attention patterns without explicit head-wise pattern-type assignment. A lightweight gate learns block importance from dense attention supervision, providing a representative learned selector under the fixed budget used in our evaluation. SpargeAttn ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) provides a training-free alternative using online attention prediction and softmax-aware filtering. FlexPrefill ( Lai et al., 2025 ) further increases flexibility by adapting both pattern type and budget without additional training . For each input and head, it chooses between vertical-slash and query-aware block selection, then determines the number of retained units using a cumulative-attention threshold. XAttention ( Xu et al., 2025 ) also performs input-dependent block selection, estimating block importance through antidiagonal sampling. Together, MInference, SeerAttention, and FlexPrefill cover the main design choices in sparse attention: vertical, slash, and block units; offline-assigned and input-adaptive pattern types; fixed and adaptive budgets; and training-free and learned selection. Their complementary mechanisms provide a suitable testbed for evaluating whether MASA gives a general scoring correction across distinct sparse attention designs, rather than an improvement confined to a single implementation .

sections.heading: 3.3 Implementation
sections.text: Our theory applies to sparse attention selection in general. In our implementation and experiments, we instantiate MASA in the sparse prefill setting, where the main cost comes from computing attention over a long prompt before decoding. This is also the setting of our baselines, including MInference ( Jiang et al., 2024a ) , SeerAttention ( Gao et al., 2025 ) , and FlexPrefill ( Lai et al., 2025 ) . MASA keeps their sparse unit definitions, sparse kernels, and budget rules unchanged, and only replaces the score used to rank candidate sparse units. All MASA scores are computed at the same profile resolution as the baselines. Thus, 𝑨 {\bm{A}} and 𝑿 {\bm{X}} in the scoring formulas denote the baseline’s profile attention map and the matching profile probe when the baseline ranks units at block or other reduced resolution. MASA therefore does not require a new full-resolution dense attention map beyond the information used for sparse-unit ranking. Structured sparse units. The direct probe is 𝑿 = 𝑽 {\bm{X}}={\bm{V}} , because the true attention output is 𝑨 ​ 𝑽 {\bm{A}}{\bm{V}} . Raw value vectors, however, can contain high-norm outliers. We therefore use norm-controlled value probes to keep value directions while reducing the effect of extreme norms. One option is soft norm balancing: 𝑿 j = 𝑽 j ( ‖ 𝑽 j ‖ 2 + ϵ ) α , 0 ≤ α ≤ 1 . {\bm{X}}_{j}=\frac{{\bm{V}}_{j}}{(\|{\bm{V}}_{j}\|_{2}+\epsilon)^{\alpha}},\qquad 0\leq\alpha\leq 1. (10) When α = 0 \alpha=0 , this is the raw value probe. When α = 1 \alpha=1 , it keeps the value direction while removing the value norm. Intermediate values keep part of the norm information while reducing the effect of high-norm outliers. Another option is norm clipping: 𝑿 j = 𝑽 j ⋅ min ⁡ ( 1 , c ‖ 𝑽 j ‖ 2 + ϵ ) , {\bm{X}}_{j}={\bm{V}}_{j}\cdot\min\left(1,\frac{c}{\|{\bm{V}}_{j}\|_{2}+\epsilon}\right), (11) where c c is a chosen percentile of value-vector norms in the profile region. This keeps normal value vectors unchanged and only clips unusually large norms. The probe view also supports more general matrix-action metrics . Appendix C shows that weighted output metrics can be written in the same form by choosing an appropriate probe 𝑿 {\bm{X}} , and that the Frobenius matrix-product error controls the spectral matrix-product error. Finally, when the baseline ranks units on a profile attention map, we build 𝑿 {\bm{X}} at the same profile resolution. For example, block-level selection uses block-pooled value probes, so that the probe matches the sparse units used by the implemented kernel .

sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: Existing sparse attention studies often differ in budgets, kernels, LLM backbones, and benchmark choices, which makes isolated comparisons hard to interpret. We therefore evaluate MASA under a controlled protocol designed to test whether the proposed matrix-approximation view improves existing sparse attention methods without changing their own settings . First, we do not evaluate MASA on a single favorable framework, but attach it to three representative sparse attention baselines with different sparse units and selection rules. Second, we do not tune the sparse budget, kernel, baseline hyperparameters, or data processing for MASA; each baseline keeps its official configuration, and MASA only replaces the sparse-unit ranking score. Third, we evaluate on the long-context benchmarks used by the original baselines, including RULER ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ) , InfiniteBench ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , and LongBench ( Bai et al., 2024b ) . This protocol directly tests whether MASA improves sparse attention under the conditions where the baselines are already designed to work well .

sections.heading: 4.1 Setups
sections.text: Baselines. We evaluate MASA by augmenting three representative sparse attention methods: MInference ( Jiang et al., 2024a ) , SeerAttention ( Gao et al., 2025 ) , and FlexPrefill ( Lai et al., 2025 ) , as discussed in Sec. 2.1 . These baselines cover vertical, slash, and block-wise sparse patterns; fixed and input-adaptive selection; fixed and adaptive budgets; and training-free and learned selection rules. This makes them a strong test bed for evaluating whether MASA is a general correction rather than a method-specific modification. Implementation. All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU with CUDA 12.6. The FlashAttention ( Dao et al., 2022 ) and Triton ( Tillet et al., 2019 ) settings follow the corresponding baseline implementations. For each sparse attention baseline, MASA uses the official code path, released weights, sparse kernels, sparse unit definitions, and budget rules. The only change is the ranking score used to select candidate sparse units. This matched setting isolates the effect of the MASA score from other engineering factors. Benchmarks. We follow the benchmark choices of the original baselines. RULER ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ) is used for all three baselines. It is a synthetic long-context benchmark with controllable sequence lengths and task types, including needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, multi-hop tracing, and aggregation. InfiniteBench ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) is used for MInference and FlexPrefill. It evaluates long-dependency understanding over contexts with an average of about 214K tokens and includes both synthetic and real-world tasks. LongBench ( Bai et al., 2024b ) is used for SeerAttention. It is a bilingual long-context benchmark covering multi-document question answering, summarization, and retrieval tasks. sections.heading: 4.3 Efficiency
sections.text: MASA replaces the baseline’s sparse-unit ranking score rather than adding a new attention component. Its only additional computation is evaluating the reduction score in Eq. ( 8 ) within the existing ranking stage. We therefore measure kernel-level latency under the same sparse settings to verify that this replacement preserves the efficiency advantage of sparse attention. Fig. 2 reports latency normalized to dense FlashAttention-2 at sequence lengths 32K, 64K, and 128K. Across MInference, SeerAttention, FlexPrefill-Llama, and FlexPrefill-Qwen, replacing the original ranking score with MASA adds empirically negligible overhead relative to the sparse attention runtime and remains far below the dense attention cost. The overhead also stays negligible at 128K, the main regime where sparse attention is needed. Therefore, MASA improves accuracy without weakening the practical efficiency of the underlying sparse attention method.

sections.text: MASA is derived from the matrix-product approximation objective in Sec. 3.2 . The remaining implementation choice is the probe matrix 𝑿 {\bm{X}} . The direct choice 𝑿 = 𝑽 {\bm{X}}={\bm{V}} gives the attention-output objective, while Sec. 3.3 also introduces norm-controlled probes to reduce the effect of high-norm value outliers. We ablate soft norm balancing in Eq. ( 10 ) and norm clipping in Eq. ( 11 ), with full length- and task-level results in Appendix F . Together with the main results in Sec. 4.2 , the probe ablation in Table 4 supports two conclusions. First, raw MASA already improves the original sparse baseline in several settings, which supports the matrix-product scoring objective itself. Second, norm control can further improve the score in settings where value-norm outliers affect sparse-unit ranking. Norm clipping is helpful for SeerAttention and FlexPrefill-Llama, while soft norm balancing is useful in some FlexPrefill settings. These trends match the probe design: MASA should preserve value directions while preventing a small number of high-norm value vectors from dominating the selection score. sections.heading: 5 Conclusion
sections.text: This paper identifies a fundamental selection mismatch in sparse attention. Existing methods usually retain large attention entries or high-mass regions, which treats the attention matrix as a bag of scalar values. However, Transformers use the attention matrix through matrix multiplication with value vectors. Therefore, sparse attention should be formulated as matrix approximation, not as entrywise attention compression. Based on this view, we propose MASA, a theory-grounded plug-in correction that ranks sparse units by their closed-form reduction in matrix-product approximation error. MASA does not change the sparse kernels, candidate sparse units, or budget rules of existing methods, making it orthogonal to low-level attention kernels and other LLM acceleration techniques as discussed in Appendix A . Across multiple sparse baselines, benchmarks, and LLM backbones, MASA gives consistent gains under matched settings with negligible latency overhead. These results support both the proposed method and the broader matrix-approximation view of sparse attention. One practical boundary of MASA is that it corrects the selection score within a given sparse attention framework. It does not search for new sparse kernels, new sparse unit families, or new budget schedules. This is also what makes the comparison clean: MASA isolates the effect of the selection objective while keeping the original sparse attention system unchanged. Future work can combine MASA with better kernel designs, adaptive budget policies, and other LLM acceleration methods, but the core message remains independent of these engineering choices: sparse attention should preserve the matrix action of attention, not blindly keep large scalar entries.

sections.heading: AI use statement
sections.text: LLMs are used to assist with grammar checking, improving writing fluency, managing computational resources and providing suggestions after the initial draft. All observations, ideas, methodologies in this paper are developed entirely by the authors. Any content generated with the help of LLMs is created under detailed author instructions and thoroughly verified by the authors before inclusion.

sections.heading: Appendix A LLM Acceleration
sections.text: LLM inference acceleration. The quadratic cost of self-attention with respect to sequence length has motivated many acceleration methods for long-context LLM inference. One line improves hardware efficiency through IO-aware or distributed attention kernels, including FlashAttention ( Dao et al., 2022 ) , FlashDecoding++ ( Hong et al., 2024 ) , and RingAttention ( Liu et al., 2024a ) . Another reduces the effective context length through retrieval, prompt compression, or context-memory mechanisms ( Borgeaud et al., 2022 ; Jiang et al., 2023b ; Jiang et al., 2024b ; Xiao et al., 2024a ) . For decoding, methods address KV-cache efficiency through paged memory management, quantization, selective cache use, and eviction ( Kwon et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Xiao et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) . Other approaches change the model architecture through recurrence, state-space models, linear attention, or hybrid designs ( Dai et al., 2019 ; Sun et al., 2023 ; Gu & Dao, 2023 ) . These approaches reduce inference cost through computation, memory, context, or architectural changes. Oracle analysis and KV-cache reduction. Gupta & Berant (2021) analyze per-query oracle approximations expressed as sparse convex combinations of value vectors, setting aside computational and memory constraints. VATP ( Guo et al., 2024 ) , CAOTE ( Goel et al., 2025 ) , and CurDKV ( Sengupta et al., 2026 ) instead address KV-cache reduction, selecting retained states through norm-weighted token importance, eviction-induced output error, and CUR-based scores, respectively. Their selection objects are approximation coefficients or cached KV states. MASA instead ranks framework-defined masks over query–key interactions for structured sparse attention computation. Sparse attention. Sparse attention reduces computation by retaining only a subset of query–key interactions ( Child et al., 2019 ; Beltagy et al., 2020 ; Zaheer et al., 2020 ; Xiao et al., 2024b ) . Methods differ in how they construct this subset: fixed local, global, or sink patterns; offline assignment of structured patterns; learned prediction of input-dependent regions; and adaptive selection budgets ( Jiang et al., 2024a ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Lai et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) . The representative sparse-prefill frameworks reviewed in Sec. 2.1 rank candidate units using attention-weight summaries or learned attention-pattern targets. These criteria estimate where attention is concentrated, rather than directly evaluating the matrix-product error reduction from retaining a candidate unit. Thus, constructing a sparse pattern family and choosing how to rank its units are distinct design questions. Position and novelty of MASA. MASA is orthogonal to sparse-kernel optimization and KV-cache storage design: it changes the selection criterion, not the execution kernel or cache representation. Within sparse attention, MASA also retains the candidate pattern family and budget rule. Pattern construction defines the admissible sparse units, the budget constrains their selection, and the kernel executes the selected interactions. MASA addresses a different question: which units should be retained to preserve the attention matrix product? MASA answers this question through matrix-approximation ranking of structured sparse units . The closed-form score in Eq. ( 7 ) measures the reduction in retained matrix-product error from selecting each candidate individually. It accounts for alignment with the target product 𝑨 ​ 𝑿 {\bm{A}}{\bm{X}} and interactions among entries within the unit, yielding a common criterion for vertical, slash, and block patterns. The implementation evaluates this criterion at the framework’s existing profile resolution through profile-matched probes and memory-safe matrix products (Sec. 3.3 ). Raw, pooled, and norm-controlled probes use the same scoring formulation without changing the value vectors consumed by the sparse kernel. This distinction is the main novelty of MASA: it connects a structured matrix-approximation objective to a common ranking mechanism within existing sparse attention systems. Rather than introducing another sparse pattern, compression policy, or execution kernel, MASA changes what makes a candidate unit important: its contribution to matrix-product preservation, not merely its attention mass. It therefore complements advances in sparse execution and memory management with a theory-grounded correction to the selection principle.

Learn more × Back to arXiv License: CC BY 4.0 arXiv:2610.10871v1 [cs.CL] 07 Oct 2026 Sparse Attention Is Matrix Approximation, Not Choosing from a Bag of Values Fang Wan Affiliation: Stony Brook University Xufeng Liu Affiliation: Stony Brook University Fan Li Affiliation: Duke University Yi Liu † † thanks: Correspondence to yi.liu.4@stonybrook.edu Affiliation: Stony Brook University Abstract Large Language Models (LLMs) achieve strong performance across many domains, but their efficiency is limited by the quadratic cost of attention with respect to prompt length. Sparse attention reduces this cost by retaining only a small fraction of query-key interactions to approximate the full attention matrix. However, existing methods are trapped in a mathematically wrong view: they simply keep large scalar entries or high-mass regions of the attention matrix. This treats the attention matrix as a bag of values, ignoring that it is used as a structured matrix whose entries jointly determine the attention output through multiplication with value vectors. We argue that this is the core conceptual issue: sparse attention should be formulated as matrix approximation, not as blindly choosing the largest values from a bag of entries. Extensive experiments across multiple sparse attention methods, benchmarks, and LLM backbones show consistent accuracy gains, supporting both MASA and the matrix-approximation view of sparse attention. 1 Introduction Large Language Models (LLMs) have achieved strong performance across a wide range of applications, from natural language processing ( Radford et al., 2018 ) to mathematical reasoning ( Ahn et al., 2024 ) , multimodal tasks ( Team et al., 2023 ) , and scientific discovery ( Zhang et al., 2025b ) . However, efficiency remains a central challenge for LLMs ( Bai et al., 2024a ) . As tasks become more complex and prompts become more structured, the input length continues to grow rapidly ( Liu et al., 2025 ) . Since attention computation has quadratic complexity with respect to the prompt length ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) , attention becomes a major bottleneck for efficient long-context inference. Sparse attention is a natural way to reduce this cost while keeping the main modeling benefit of attention. Prior work has observed that attention matrices often contain sparse and structured patterns ( Jiang et al., 2024a ) , suggesting that only a small fraction of query-key interactions is needed to approximate full attention. Based on this observation, many methods select a sparse subset of the attention matrix under a compute budget. Early approaches use fixed or predefined patterns: Sliding Window Attention ( Jiang et al., 2023a ) restricts each query to a local context window, while MInference ( Jiang et al., 2024a ) approximates attention using vertical lines, slash lines, and blocks. Other methods make the selection input-aware: SeerAttention ( Gao et al., 2025 ) learns to predict block-sparse attention patterns, and Quest ( Tang et al., 2024 ) retrieves query-aware key pages. More recent methods further adapt the sparse budget, such as FlexPrefill ( Lai et al., 2025 ) , which decides when to stop selecting additional sparse units, and Tactic ( Zhu et al., 2025 ) , which adjusts the budget through clustering and distribution fitting. Despite these different designs, the final selection rule remains ultimately magnitude-driven: sparse attention methods keep large scalar entries or high-mass regions of the attention matrix. This selection principle has a mathematical mismatch. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , a candidate with much larger mass can preserve the matrix product substantially worse under the same sparse budget. Magnitude-based selection treats the attention matrix as a bag of scalar values, whereas Transformers use it as a structured matrix acting on value vectors through matrix multiplication ( Vaswani et al., 2017 ) . Therefore, the right question is not which entries of the attention matrix are largest, but which selected entries best preserve the matrix product that produces the attention output. In other words, sparse attention should be formulated as matrix approximation, not as blindly choosing the largest values from a bag of entries. Based on this view, we propose M atrix A pproximation S parse A ttention ( MASA ), a theory-grounded plug-in correction for sparse attention. MASA keeps the sparse units, kernels, and budgets of existing sparse attention methods, but replaces their raw attention-mass ranking with a closed-form score derived from matrix-product approximation error. This changes the selection target from preserving large entries of the attention matrix to preserving the matrix action that determines the attention output. As a result, MASA can be added to diverse sparse attention frameworks without changing their implementation interface. Figure 1: A minimal two-column counterexample. We identify a long-standing selection mismatch in sparse attention: existing magnitude-based rules approximate the attention matrix entrywise, while the Transformer uses attention through matrix multiplication. We provide a matrix-approximation view that gives the correct selection objective. • Method. Broader LLM acceleration methods are discussed in Appendix A . 2.1 Related Work MInference ( Jiang et al., 2024a ) is a training-free framework that exploits multiple structured patterns through offline head-wise assignment . It searches among A-shaped, vertical-slash, and block-sparse patterns for each attention head. The assigned pattern type and budget remain fixed, while sparse indices are constructed dynamically for each input. MoA ( Fu et al., 2025 ) similarly uses offline configuration, but sets head- and layer-specific sliding-window spans. SeerAttention ( Gao et al., 2025 ) instead learns input-dependent sparse layouts within a block-based representation . GPU-friendly blocks can approximate different attention patterns without explicit head-wise pattern-type assignment. A lightweight gate learns block importance from dense attention supervision, providing a representative learned selector under the fixed budget used in our evaluation. SpargeAttn ( Zhang et al., 2025a ) provides a training-free alternative using online attention prediction and softmax-aware filtering. FlexPrefill ( Lai et al., 2025 ) further increases flexibility by adapting both pattern type and budget without additional training . For each input and head, it chooses between vertical-slash and query-aware block selection, then determines the number of retained units using a cumulative-attention threshold. XAttention ( Xu et al., 2025 ) also performs input-dependent block selection, estimating block importance through antidiagonal sampling. Together, MInference, SeerAttention, and FlexPrefill cover the main design choices in sparse attention: vertical, slash, and block units; offline-assigned and input-adaptive pattern types; fixed and adaptive budgets; and training-free and learned selection. For example, block-level selection uses block-pooled value probes, so that the probe matches the sparse units used by the implemented kernel . 4 Experiments Existing sparse attention studies often differ in budgets, kernels, LLM backbones, and benchmark choices, which makes isolated comparisons hard to interpret. We therefore evaluate MASA under a controlled protocol designed to test whether the proposed matrix-approximation view improves existing sparse attention methods without changing their own settings . First, we do not evaluate MASA on a single favorable framework, but attach it to three representative sparse attention baselines with different sparse units and selection rules. Second, we do not tune the sparse budget, kernel, baseline hyperparameters, or data processing for MASA; each baseline keeps its official configuration, and MASA only replaces the sparse-unit ranking score. Third, we evaluate on the long-context benchmarks used by the original baselines, including RULER ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ) , InfiniteBench ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) , and LongBench ( Bai et al., 2024b ) . This protocol directly tests whether MASA improves sparse attention under the conditions where the baselines are already designed to work well . 4.1 Setups Baselines. We evaluate MASA by augmenting three representative sparse attention methods: MInference ( Jiang et al., 2024a ) , SeerAttention ( Gao et al., 2025 ) , and FlexPrefill ( Lai et al., 2025 ) , as discussed in Sec. 2.1 . These baselines cover vertical, slash, and block-wise sparse patterns; fixed and input-adaptive selection; fixed and adaptive budgets; and training-free and learned selection rules. This makes them a strong test bed for evaluating whether MASA is a general correction rather than a method-specific modification. Implementation. All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA H100 80GB GPU with CUDA 12.6. The FlashAttention ( Dao et al., 2022 ) and Triton ( Tillet et al., 2019 ) settings follow the corresponding baseline implementations. For each sparse attention baseline, MASA uses the official code path, released weights, sparse kernels, sparse unit definitions, and budget rules. The only change is the ranking score used to select candidate sparse units. This matched setting isolates the effect of the MASA score from other engineering factors. Benchmarks. We follow the benchmark choices of the original baselines. RULER ( Hsieh et al., 2024 ) is used for all three baselines. It is a synthetic long-context benchmark with controllable sequence lengths and task types, including needle-in-a-haystack retrieval, multi-hop tracing, and aggregation. InfiniteBench ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) is used for MInference and FlexPrefill. LongBench ( Bai et al., 2024b ) is used for SeerAttention. It is a bilingual long-context benchmark covering multi-document question answering, summarization, and retrieval tasks. Existing methods usually retain large attention entries or high-mass regions, which treats the attention matrix as a bag of scalar values. However, Transformers use the attention matrix through matrix multiplication with value vectors. Therefore, sparse attention should be formulated as matrix approximation, not as entrywise attention compression. Based on this view, we propose MASA, a theory-grounded plug-in correction that ranks sparse units by their closed-form reduction in matrix-product approximation error. MASA does not change the sparse kernels, candidate sparse units, or budget rules of existing methods, making it orthogonal to low-level attention kernels and other LLM acceleration techniques as discussed in Appendix A . Across multiple sparse baselines, benchmarks, and LLM backbones, MASA gives consistent gains under matched settings with negligible latency overhead. These results support both the proposed method and the broader matrix-approximation view of sparse attention. One practical boundary of MASA is that it corrects the selection score within a given sparse attention framework. It does not search for new sparse kernels, new sparse unit families, or new budget schedules. This is also what makes the comparison clean: MASA isolates the effect of the selection objective while keeping the original sparse attention system unchanged. Future work can combine MASA with better kernel designs, adaptive budget policies, and other LLM acceleration methods, but the core message remains independent of these engineering choices: sparse attention should preserve the matrix action of attention, not blindly keep large scalar entries. The quadratic cost of self-attention with respect to sequence length has motivated many acceleration methods for long-context LLM inference. One line improves hardware efficiency through IO-aware or distributed attention kernels, including FlashAttention ( Dao et al., 2022 ) , FlashDecoding++ ( Hong et al., 2024 ) , and RingAttention ( Liu et al., 2024a ) . Another reduces the effective context length through retrieval, prompt compression, or context-memory mechanisms ( Borgeaud et al., 2022 ; Jiang et al., 2023b ; Jiang et al., 2024b ; Xiao et al., 2024a ) . For decoding, methods address KV-cache efficiency through paged memory management, quantization, selective cache use, and eviction ( Kwon et al., 2023 ; Liu et al., 2024b ; Xiao et al., 2025 ; Zhang et al., 2023 ) . Other approaches change the model architecture through recurrence, state-space models, linear attention, or hybrid designs ( Dai et al., 2019 ; Sun et al., 2023 ; Gu & Dao, 2023 ) . These approaches reduce inference cost through computation, memory, context, or architectural changes. Oracle analysis and KV-cache reduction. Gupta & Berant (2021) analyze per-query oracle approximations expressed as sparse convex combinations of value vectors, setting aside computational and memory constraints. VATP ( Guo et al., 2024 ) , CAOTE ( Goel et al., 2025 ) , and CurDKV ( Sengupta et al., 2026 ) instead address KV-cache reduction, selecting retained states through norm-weighted token importance, eviction-induced output error, and CUR-based scores, respectively. Their selection objects are approximation coefficients or cached KV states. MASA instead ranks framework-defined masks over query–key interactions for structured sparse attention computation. Sparse attention. Sparse attention reduces computation by retaining only a subset of query–key interactions ( Child et al., 2019 ; Beltagy et al., 2020 ; Zaheer et al., 2020 ; Xiao et al., 2024b ) . Methods differ in how they construct this subset: fixed local, global, or sink patterns; offline assignment of structured patterns; learned prediction of input-dependent regions; and adaptive selection budgets ( Jiang et al., 2024a ; Gao et al., 2025 ; Lai et al., 2025 ; Zhu et al., 2025 ) . The representative sparse-prefill frameworks reviewed in Sec. 2.1 rank candidate units using attention-weight summaries or learned attention-pattern targets. These criteria estimate where attention is concentrated, rather than directly evaluating the matrix-product error reduction from retaining a candidate unit. Thus, constructing a sparse pattern family and choosing how to rank its units are distinct design questions. Position and novelty of MASA. MASA is orthogonal to sparse-kernel optimization and KV-cache storage design: it changes the selection criterion, not the execution kernel or cache representation. Within sparse attention, MASA also retains the candidate pattern family and budget rule. Pattern construction defines the admissible sparse units, the budget constrains their selection, and the kernel executes the selected interactions. MASA addresses a different question: which units should be retained to preserve the attention matrix product? MASA answers this question through matrix-approximation ranking of structured sparse units . The closed-form score in Eq. ( 7 ) measures the reduction in retained matrix-product error from selecting each candidate individually. It accounts for alignment with the target product 𝑨 ​ 𝑿 {\bm{A}}{\bm{X}} and interactions among entries within the unit, yielding a common criterion for vertical, slash, and block patterns. The implementation evaluates this criterion at the framework’s existing profile resolution through profile-matched probes and memory-safe matrix products (Sec. 3.3 ). Raw, pooled, and norm-controlled probes use the same scoring formulation without changing the value vectors consumed by the sparse kernel. This distinction is the main novelty of MASA: it connects a structured matrix-approximation objective to a common ranking mechanism within existing sparse attention systems. Rather than introducing another sparse pattern, compression policy, or execution kernel, MASA changes what makes a candidate unit important: its contribution to matrix-product preservation, not merely its attention mass. It therefore complements advances in sparse execution and memory management with a theory-grounded correction to the selection principle.
